Male infertility Immunosuppressive treatment with corticosteroids has been given for male infertility (p.2080) due to low-grade auto-immune orchitis.1 Corticosteroids have also been used in men with autoantibodies to spermatozoa. Various regimens have been tried, such as giving the man a corti- costeroid for a set number of days during the partner’s menstrual cycle, or giving a continuous low-dose for sev- eral months.2 However, there is a lack of evidence of ben- efit from substantial controlled trials and the use of corti- costeroids is not generally recommended. They might, however, be considered for men with autoantibodies who have failed assisted reproductive techniques.1 1. Haidl G. Management strategies for male factor infertility. Drugs 2002; 62: 1741–53. 2. Lombardo F, et al. Antisperm immunity in natural and assisted reproduction. Hum Reprod Update 2001; 7: 450–6. Malignant neoplasms Corticosteroids are extensively prescribed in malignant disease for the relief of pain, nerve compression, or raised intracranial pressure; to alleviate dyspnoea, effusion, or hypercalcaemia; to counteract adverse effects of other therapies such as antineoplastic-induced nausea and vom- iting or radiation-induced inflammation; and in the man- agement of cachexia and to improve mood and sense of well-being.1 In addition they form an important part of multidrug anticancer regimens used for various haemato- logical malignancies such as acute lymphoblastic leukae- mia (p.651) and Hodgkin’s disease (p.655). In contrast, it has been postulated that the use of corticosteroids in pa- tients with solid, non-haematological tumours might in- duce resistance in cancer cells to cytotoxic therapy, and in- crease the risk of treatment failure, although clinical evidence for this is lacking.2 1. Twycross R. The risks and benefits of corticosteroids in ad- vanced cancer. Drug Safety 1994; 11: 163–78. 2. Rutz HP. Effects of corticosteroid use on treatment of solid tu- mours.
